newsitem.title: TAJIKISTAN: Peace talks start, fighting dies in Tajikistan.
newsitem.headline: Peace talks start, fighting dies in Tajikistan.

text.p: There was no fighting in Tajikistan on Wednesday as President Imomali Rakhmonov and mutinous Colonel Makhmud Khudoyberdyev started peace talks mediated by Russian peacekeepers in the former Soviet republic.
Russia's Itar-Tass and Interfax news agencies, quoting Russian military sources, said the meeting was held at a Russian military base in the capital Dushanbe.
There was no independent confirmation or details.
Forces loyal to Rakhmonov have been battling the renegade colonel south of Dushanbe since Saturday.

"Rakhmonov and Khudoyberdyev spoke by telephone last night," Zafar Saidov, Rakhmonov's press secretary, told Reuters by telephone in the capital Dushanbe. "Both sides have said the conflict can only be resolved by peaceful means".
He added that the Fakhrobad valley, 25 km (15 miles) south of Dushanbe and where government forces exchanged mortar and rocket fire with Khudoyberdyev's troops on Tuesday, had been quiet overnight.
Saidov said the colonel had begun to withdraw some of his armour to his headquarters near Kurgan Tyube, about 110 km (80 miles) south of Dushanbe.
At a post held by Rakhmonov's presidential guard about 14 km (9 miles) south of Dushanbe, no clashes could be heard.

"There were a few rounds exchanged overnight but otherwise it's been quiet," said Tajikistan's deputy interior minister, Nikolai Madzhar, in combat fatigues and toying with a walkie-talkie at the post.
"There won't be peace talks," said Madzhar. "There will only be Khudoyberdyev's surrender".
But he would not confirm that Khudoyberdyev had withdrawn his forces from the contested valley while other soldiers at the post said the rebel colonel's men were still there.
The eruption of fighting on Saturday is not linked to the republic's armed Islamic opposition, with whom Rakhmonov signed a peace accord in June aimed at ending four years of civil war.
The latest clashes show Rakhmonov's already weak grip on power even weaker, leaving the impoverished republic far from the stability craved by its 5.7 million population.
Gun law has seen Tajikistan divided up into a complicated patchwork of independent fiefdoms under the control of armed groups like those in neighbouring Afghanistan.

Khudoyberdyev, 34, the politically ambitious commander of an elite government armoured brigade, has mutinied twice before in as many years. He has also been a vociferous critic of the peace struck with the Islamists.
He moved his armour towards Dushanbe at the weekend after fighting broke out between between two rival warlords in the capital but his motives for doing so are clouded in speculation.
Khudoyberdyev said on Tuesday he had no plans to take the capital and said he had been provoked by what he said was the presidential guard's move on his territory in the south.
He lost control of a strategically important aluminium smelter west of the capital to the presidential guard on Monday.

"He is thought to have long term ambitions for national leadership," said a Western diplomat on condition of anonymity. "But he appeared recently only to be building up his local power base in the south".
"Khudoyberdyev's flexed his muscles and won concessions before but my feeling is that this time he miscalculated," the diplomat said.
Russia, which deploys 20,000 troops in the Central Asian state and which fears unrest along its unstable southern rim, has been cautious in its reaction to the fighting.
On Tuesday, the predominantly Russian peacekeeping force in Tajikistan fielded by the Commonwealth of Independent States said it would stay neutral and take no part in the conflict.
